topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and mathematics

outline.topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
outline.target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and mathematics

sections.title: Introduction: The Binary Basics (1 minute)
sections.content: Define the binary system using a 'Light Switch' analogy. Explain how each bit represents a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8...), showing that any decimal number is a unique sum of powers of 2.
sections.example: Represent the number 13 as 8 + 4 + 1, visualized as three lit bulbs (ON-OFF-ON-ON) corresponding to positions 2^3, 2^2, and 2^0.

sections.title: Mapping Towers of Hanoi to Binary (1.5 minutes)
sections.content: Introduce the puzzle: Moving n disks takes 2^n - 1 moves. Demonstrate that the disk movement sequence follows a binary counting pattern (Gray Code logic).
sections.example: For 3 disks, the total moves are 2^3 - 1 = 7. Show a table where move numbers 1 through 7 correspond to the disk that moves: 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1.

sections.title: Visualizing the Algorithm (1.5 minutes)
sections.content: Connect the binary representation of the move count (1 to 7) to the actual physical disk movement. Specifically, the disk moved is determined by the position of the least significant bit that changes in binary.
sections.example: A robotic arm (character: 'Bit the Bot') moves Disk 1 on odd steps (1, 3, 5, 7), Disk 2 on steps 2 and 6, and Disk 3 on step 4.

sections.title: Synthesis and Application (1 minute)
sections.content: Summarize how binary isn't just for counting, but serves as an instruction set for recursive problems. Conclude by showing how this logic scales to any number of disks.
sections.example: Animation showing the disks moving synchronously with a binary counter clock, transforming the complex puzzle into a simple rhythmic pulse.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Binary Basics (1 minute)
lecture_lines: Binary represents numbers using switches, ON or OFF.
Each switch corresponds to a power of two.
Thirteen is eight plus four plus one.
Any decimal number uniquely sums these powers.
animations: Create a neon-green (#00FF00) circle representing a bit.
Move the bit circle to the center of the screen.
Flash the bit circle in bright yellow (#FFFF00) to signal activity.

storyboard.title: Mapping Towers of Hanoi to Binary (1.5 minutes)
lecture_lines: Moving N disks requires two to the N minus one moves.
Seven moves are needed for three disks.
Sequence counts binary like a rhythmic clock.
animations: Draw three vertical stacks of varying sizes (#FF0000).
Place a numeric binary label (#00FFFF) beside each stack.
Animate the stacks transforming into a binary sequence (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Visualizing the Algorithm (1.5 minutes)
lecture_lines: Binary patterns dictate exactly which disk moves next.
Bit the Bot moves Disk One on odd steps.
Bit the Bot moves Disk Two on steps two, six.
Bit the Bot moves Disk Three on step four.
Movement follows the least significant changing bit.
animations: Visualize a recursive flow arrow (#00FF00) moving between disks.
Highlight the smallest disk in bright cyan (#00FFFF).
Shift the disks using a smooth translation animation (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Synthesis and Application (1 minute)
lecture_lines: Binary is an instruction set for recursive puzzles.
Logical pulse controls every disk transition.
This rhythm scales to any number of disks.
animations: Display a combined binary tree (#FFFFFF) on screen.
Highlight the root node in bright magenta (#FF00FF).
Animate the nodes fading into a final summary diagram.
